idea: This is Nebula Vault, my Freestyle Week project: a spacecraft salvage box with a hidden mechanical latch.
The player aligns three orbital signals with alternating turns, then repeats a short, long, short pulse rhythm.
An encoder is the main control. An OLED gives clues, and a ring of twelve lights supplies the timing pattern.
Solving the puzzle commands a servo to release the lid. A manual access slot provides a fallback.
These are renders of the actual project CAD, not footage of a finished device. Physical fit and motion remain untested.
progress: Here is the Nebula Vault electronics and firmware walkthrough.
A Pico reads the encoder and push switch, drives the light ring and OLED, and commands the servo.
The wiring uses a five volt AHCT buffer for pixel data and the servo control signal. The OLED remains at three point three volts.
The puzzle logic is separate from the hardware layer, so its state transitions can be checked on a desktop.
The package records fifteen passing logic tests. That is existing software evidence, not a physical electronics test.
late: This reel shows the recorded software simulation supplied with Nebula Vault. It is not a physical hardware demonstration.
The trace starts with arming, then clockwise alignment to three, counterclockwise to eight, and clockwise to one.
After pulse playback, the ideal event sequence reproduces intervals of four hundred fifty, nine hundred, and four hundred fifty milliseconds.
The recorded puzzle engine reaches its open state. That result establishes logic behavior for this event sequence only.
It does not establish servo torque, current draw, printed fit, light diffusion, or mechanical reliability.
closing: This is the Nebula Vault design submission walkthrough.
The actual source package includes editable parametric CAD, seven printable parts, a labeled wiring diagram, MicroPython firmware, and a vendor priced bill of materials.
The enclosure separates the electronics bay and storage area. A servo horn extension engages the lid keeper.
The package records digital collision checks and logic tests. The visuals here are source diagrams and CAD renders, not physical photographs.
Printing, fit checks, wiring, servo calibration, electrical measurements, and endurance testing still need to happen.
